title: Exhibitions and trade fairs: property, stands and liability
excerpt: What a business in Moldova should prepare for a fair: inventory, ownership, transport, assembly, demonstrations and insurance condition checks.
imageAlt: An exhibitor team checking a modern trade fair stand and demonstration equipment records

seo.title: Exhibition and trade fair insurance in Moldova | ING Broker
seo.description: Separate exhibits, rented stands, transport and visitor liability. Prepare the complete participation schedule before comparing possible insurance conditions.
seo.keywords: exhibition insurance Moldova, trade fair insurance, exhibits insurance, stand liability, exhibition transport risk

author: ING Broker editorial team
content:
Taking part in a trade fair involves transporting property, assembling the stand, using equipment temporarily and welcoming visitors. These situations cannot be reduced to a single expression, “exhibition insurance”. For a company in the Republic of Moldova, assessment starts with the inventory, ownership of the goods and the stages of participation. An office policy should not be assumed to apply to every object temporarily moved into an exhibition hall.

This material helps exhibitors and organisers prepare for a risk assessment. It does not confirm the availability of a special product for every fair or promise cover for every instance of damage or missing property. Conditions and acceptance of the risk must be checked with the provider of the solution being assessed. The broker can explain available options without turning event rules into an insurance policy or guaranteeing the outcome of a claim.

Who organises and who exhibits?

Identify the event organiser, participating company, hall owner and stand contractors. These roles may belong to different companies. Their contracts may contain different obligations that competent advisers need to check. Do not assume insurance announced by the organiser automatically protects each exhibitor's property or every activity at the stand. Ask for the relevant documents and explanations.

For joint participation, identify the company owning each item and who uses it. A machine borrowed from a partner does not become the exhibitor's own property because it appears in the presentation catalogue. Record who is responsible for each contractual relationship and keep the information in a controlled shared file. Do not publish partners' documents in a commercial form simply to demonstrate the size of the stand.

Inventories must describe real items

Prepare a list of exhibits, demonstration products, modular furniture and electronic equipment. Use identifiers, serial numbers and administrative photographs where necessary and permitted. Separate objects offered for sale from those only being displayed. Do not declare the same value for every unit if the documents show different circumstances. Book value and replacement cost may need separate explanations when assessing a proposal.

Explain whether an exhibit is unique, made to order or difficult to repair. For artwork or fragile objects, ask for their particular requirements to be checked before transport. Packaging designed for display should not automatically be considered suitable for travel. Technical assessment, valuation and insurance are separate questions. Keep ownership and value documents without presenting an invented figure as a professional valuation.

Transport to the fair and back

Describe who takes custody of the goods, the vehicle used, the route and any intermediate storage. Ask for handover and receipt points to be clarified. Do not confuse the carrier's liability with insurance for the transported goods. A fair lasting three days can involve a longer exposure if exhibits leave the warehouse well beforehand and return later. Use the full schedule of the goods' movement.

Before loading, keep records of consignments and the condition of the objects, following suitable procedures. Do not open or alter sensitive packaging simply for a photograph requested for a commercial enquiry. Follow the competent providers' instructions concerning transport documents. When discussing insurance, ask expressly about transport, handling and stops. Do not assume all are included merely because an item appears in the inventory.

Assembly and dismantling are separate stages

Identify who installs the stand, who connects the equipment and who confirms handover. This article does not provide instructions for assembly, electrical work or suspending objects. Such work needs to be organised through appropriate specialists and procedures. For risk assessment, describe the actual activities and their timing, including external contractors' work and any work continuing after the hall opens.

Check which items belong to the installer, the exhibitor and the venue. If a contractor presents a liability policy, read the activities and limits before assuming it addresses every instance of damage. An assembly invoice is not equivalent to confirmation of insurance. Keep handover documents and observations about the condition of the goods, without drawing improvised legal conclusions.

Demonstrations change risk questions

State whether products remain in display cases or operate in demonstrations. Working equipment, visitor testing and distributed samples raise different questions. Do not use a static description for interactive activity. Check actual conditions and do not treat safety instructions as formalities replaced by insurance.

Record who supervises and what participants are told. Do not replace product documentation with technical or medical rules from this article. Discuss programme changes before assuming the original assessment remains appropriate. Visitor claims require liability assessment separate from your own exhibits.

Property left overnight

Describe storage while the hall is closed and who controls access. Do not publicly disclose security systems, codes or vulnerabilities. Request necessary assessment information and use an appropriate channel. A guard does not confirm compensation for every shortage or identical supervision of all property.

Organise handovers between team members. If items move into separate storage, record that stage and check applicable documents. Do not retrospectively complete a handover to eliminate uncertainty. A real timeline is more useful than an apparently complete but unsupported file.

Liability toward visitors and other stands

Separate damage to your property from harm alleged by another person. A stand component, demonstration object or contractor activity may require liability questions. Examples do not determine fault or acceptance. Ask how exhibitor, installer and organiser policies relate, if present.

Check fair rules' insurance requirements before sending a certificate. A similar document name does not confirm every requirement is met. Compare limits, period, entity and activities. Obtain legal help for broader obligations. A broker email cannot modify liability accepted in a participation agreement.

Cancellation and damaged property are different

A fair can be rescheduled without damage, while an exhibit can break during an otherwise continuing event. Separate deposits, transport expenditure, repairs and possible lost revenue. Do not assume one policy resolves every category. Request each need against relevant documents and circumstances.

A premium is the amount paid for insurance. A deductible is the part of a loss borne by the insured under the contract. Read these together with the limits and exclusions, meaning situations or risks for which the contract provides no cover. A small payment says little about accepted property, periods or operations. Another exhibitor's rate is not your offer, and complete budget recovery should not be promised.

Example: demonstration machinery at a fair

A company brings a small machine, two screens and presentation products. The machine is borrowed, screens owned and stand supplied by the installer. This is illustrative, not a real customer. The team separates ownership and records movement, assembly, demonstration and return without assuming acceptance.

The person responsible notices that the initial file described only static objects. Before opening, they explain that the machine will be used in demonstrations and ask for the relevant conditions to be clarified. If a problem occurs, the team keeps records and follows the appropriate procedures. The updated description identifies who uses the machine, when and under what arrangement with its owner. This information is more useful for assessment than an enquiry giving only the fair's name and the value of the stand.

A separate sheet for each important item

A general stand photograph may not identify property sufficiently. For important demonstration equipment, record its name, number, owner, supported value and handover to transport staff. Identify accompanying accessories and packaging. This clarifies assessment scope without guaranteeing a value or incident will be accepted.

For borrowed items, distinguish the owner's requested value from the amount for which your contract makes the company responsible. Explain whether consumable samples are displayed, distributed or demonstrated. “Fair materials” conceals important differences between machinery, furniture, goods and consumables.

On return, the same record can show condition, received accessories and observations. Keep each handover where several teams use equipment. Do not alter documents retrospectively or publish serial numbers and commercial values openly. The full file goes only to justified assessment participants.

How to check property returning after the fair

When the exhibition closes, have the responsible people compare the returned property with the departure inventory. Separate items sold, samples distributed and equipment returned. Do not put every difference into a single note labelled “fair consumption”. For a missing or damaged item, retain documents and the timeline without automatically drawing conclusions about liability or compensation. This organisation also helps prepare the next exhibition: the company knows which inventory remains and which items should not be copied from an old list. Administrative records do not confirm cover for an incident. That question must be checked in the applicable documents.

Frequently asked questions about fairs and exhibitions

Does hall insurance automatically protect my exhibits?

Do not assume so. Check the subject and insured parties. Exhibitor property, organiser liability and venue ownership may be treated separately.

Should borrowed property be described?

Yes. Identify owner and conditions of use for accurate assessment. Do not declare it owned without documents. Request the exact necessary list from the provider assessed.

Is the public opening period sufficient?

Check transport, storage, assembly and return, not only attendance. This article does not establish automatic inclusion within one policy.

Which documents should I prepare?

Inventory, supported values, full programme, relevant contracts and demonstrations. Do not initially send unnecessary personal or confidential records.
